newsitem.title: USA: Traders see Japanese continuing to buy U.S. debt.
newsitem.headline: Traders see Japanese continuing to buy U.S. debt.

text.p: Some traders disputed a report published in the Wall Street Journal on Wednesday that Japanese buying of U.S. Treasuries may decline going forward.

In its "Heard on the Street" column, the Journal quoted an economist saying Japanese institutions, historically major buyers of Treasuries, would slow their bond purchases. But U.S. traders on Wednesday appeared to doubt that assertion.

"If you would assume the Treasury market is not going to go down and the dollar is going to remain firm, then I don't know where his logic is coming from," said James Kenney, head government securities trader at Prudential Securities Inc.

The Journal quoted Robert Hormats, vice chairman of Goldman Sachs International, saying "I think Japanese institutions will slow their purchases, which could begin to push up interest rates. It could be the Achilles' heel of the bond and stock markets."
The 30-year Treasury bond opened sharply lower Wednesday, in part because of the report, analysts said. The losses steepened later as stocks also opened in the minus column.
Foreign governments, including Japan, have bought at least three-quarters of new U.S. government securities issued in the past year, the Journal said.

It said concern about the future of Japanese buying began to build in early November, when Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara told a Japanese publication "the adjustment in the yen's strength looks just about over."
Japan had been buying foreign government securities as part of a two-year program to devalue the yen, the Journal story said.
And while Hormats was said to have asserted the buying spree might be ending, traders said Japanese investment should continue its ebb and flow pattern.
"Twice a year we get the Japanese investment going down, twice a year we get it going up," said Michael McClure, head of government securities trading at Zions First National Bank Capital Markets.
A temporary dip in Japanese bond buying makes sense, traders said.
"The fact is, the amount of Treasuries the Japanese bought in October was enormous," Kenney said. "I didn't think for a moment that pattern would continue."
Kenney said Hormats' reported assertion is worth consideration, even if it seems implausible.

"He may be making a valid point, it's tough to say," Kenney said. "Maybe he's way ahead of the market on this call, and maybe the Japanese will stop buying somewhere down the road, but I don't see it at the moment."

Marc Chandler, senior foreign exchange analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said one thing to consider when analyzing the flow of foreign investment into U.S. markets is the balance between public and private purchasing.
"The fact that the mix ... is somewhat more in the direction of private than previously thought underscores the attractiveness of U.S. assets," Chandler said in a report.
"As today's equity and bond sell-off is global in scope, it may be misguided to read into it a change in attitude toward U.S. markets in particular," Chandler said.
